title: I do not understand why Argylle wasn't received better

commenti.body: I imagine it had something to do with the deceptive advertising. If you make it look like Henry Cavill and Dua Lipa are the stars of your movie people are gonna be disappointed when they aren't.

Haha, the idea that critics gave bad reviews to Argylle because they were comparing it to Casablanca or Citizen Kane is quite funny. Sometimes a film is just bad. But we all have those bad movies we enjoy from time to time. Nothing new here. But no need to come up with silly arguments to justify our guilty pleasures either.

I thought the film had moments of fun, but I mostly didn't like it, because to heavily paraphrase Syndrome from The Incredibles... "when everything's a plot twist, nothing is."

While I like a wacky film, this just seemed wacky for the sake of being wacky, to me. So, it didn't grab me as I would have liked.

Critics aren't comparing films to Casablanca and Citizen Kane. They're simply giving their subjective opinions the same way we are. The only difference is that they are getting paid.

I'm glad you liked it though!

I feel that in certain genres films are well received even if they aren't really good based on general criteria, like a funny comedy or a scary horror movie. I haven't seen Argylle but it might suffer from being ambiguous whether it's a parody or a "real" movie, just based on what I've read.

I hadn't really thought of that. Makes sense. Although Henry Cavill was in it quite a bit, he was advertised as the main character, which was a bit of a draw for me but I would have seen it without him as well.

Critics don’t compare everything to Casablanca or Citizen Kane. We just want things to feel functional. And a lot of Argylle is cheap. Like the “twist” of Sam Rockwell saying she needs a bullet in her head but that’s actually only because he doesn’t like her fake persona and loves who she really is. Or the idea that you can just attach knives to your shoes and skate expertly on oil. 

If the movie was more outrageous, like Scott Pilgrim over the top, then you can get away with that stuff. But for how otherwise grounded it is…the knives in the boots is painful.

You compare it to other fun spy action comedies like Mr and Mrs Smith or Austin Powers or Burn After Reading, even something not that great like Get Smart, and it feels childish in comparison.

Indeed, you have to adjust your expectations and consider the film on what it set out to achieve. Something super ambitious that fails (think Book of Henry) is much worse than something with a low-budget but made with heart (I don’t know, think Tremors, can’t think of a recent example right now).

"Basically, I understand why the critics were tough on it (because they compare everything to Casablanca and Citizen Kane) but why didn't people like it?"

No they don't. Unless it's relevant to do so. Just because you liked the film doesn't mean you have to be snarky and dishonest about how critics view the film.

Secondly, critics are people too, they're no different from you or I except that they (usually) get paid for their subjective opinion. 

Thirdly, opinions are subjective. You liked it? Awesome. Others probably did too. And some other probably had the opposing view. You like what you like and you don't have to understand the views of others.

Argylle was not a boring movie, and I don’t think its relative predictability (despite the numerous “twists”) was a flaw. Even the occasional plot holes only bothered me a bit. I can see people watching it and having a fine time, but I can't understand people concluding that it's actually a good movie.  
The biggest thing I took issue with was the tone. The plot and dialogue was silly, fun and absurd, but the performances didn’t seem to lean into that at all and most of the settings didn’t feel very “heightened”, so it felt like the movie was taking itself seriously a lot of the time. If it had been fully and completely unapologetically silly I think I would’ve enjoyed it a lot more. It was almost disorienting for me; even though the writing was so silly that it felt like *everyone* had to be in on the joke, the movie still never managed to make me feel like *anyone* was in on the joke.  
One thing I did find to be just flat-out bad though, unrelated to that particular issue, were some of the shot choices. I found Ellie’s POV shots to be horrendous and the back-and-forth between Sam Rockwell and Henry Cavill, while a fine enough idea, seemed extraordinarily clunky in its execution. I don’t need a handful of shots of Ellie being confused or any weird slo-motion shots, and I sure as hell don’t need POV shots of Ellie blinking.  
Some other various critiques:  
\- I have no idea what’s bad about the bad guys. It seems like they reference them being involved in assassinations as though that’s supposed to automatically make them bad or something? I just don’t get it.  
\- I couldn’t tell what I was supposed to think of the Argylle books - they seem really schlocky but everyone seems to treat them like they’re genuinely good quality and not just popcorn fare.  
\- I found like the romance between Howard and Rockwell oddly sudden and shoehorned. They worked together as colleagues but I just didn’t feel any romantic connection between them at all. It seemed to just come out of nowhere and definitely detracted from the movie.  
\- I also didn’t feel any investment to the characters (except Alfie I guess, I don’t care if the CGI was bad I’m a sucker for a good kitty) - our leads were decently likable, I guess, but I just didn’t really care about them.   
\- The needle drops were all just “meh” at best. Instead of the music making a moment feel more epic or adding some comedy to the scene it was just there. Every time.  
\- This may seem like a silly complaint, but I thought Bryce Dallas Howard looked horrible in the third act. It was great on Due Lipa, but that dress color and the hair color/style just doesn’t work at all with her (yes, she looked good as Gwen Stacy, but that was a very different shade of blonde). It genuinely put a cloud over the third act for me - and what’s even worse is that the callback didn’t make sense! Why would she adopt the same hair/dress as Dua Lipa’s character?

I wasn't being snarky, I was being funny. At least I was trying to be. Most people didn't recognise the sarcasm. I know they don't literally compare to these two films. I was just using it as an example of how critics can sometimes unfairly judge films. That's all. 

You don't have to understand the views of others but, I wanted to though, otherwise I wouldn't have made the post. Now I know that most people didn't and that's okay.

Yeah, the writing could have been better. I feel like there were definitely scenes that could have been better written to fit into the movie better, including the ice-skating scene. Which was ridiculous. 

I didn't think it was very grounded personally but mostly because I went in expecting a ridiculous film and that's what it was. It felt very off the wall which allowed me to suspend the necessary disbelief to enjoy the wackier scenes. 

I wouldn't really compare it to those films personally. It wasn't trying to emulate those. I'd compare it to the rest of Matthew Vaughn's work and it's basically the same vibe. That's why I enjoyed it.

I could see it as a good movie because I like Matthew Vaughn's movies and it's basically the same thing. If you go in expecting it to be like Kingsman then you'll like it I think. 

I think the reason why it worked was *because* everyone took it seriously. Think of Nicolas Cage in *Kick Ass*, would his character have been funny if he played it funny? No. He had to play it straight for it to work. The seriousness of the acting allowed the ludicrousness to shine through. At least in my opinion. It's the same with this, if people had been in on the joke then it would have just become a standard spy parody which may or may not have worked. I'm not sure. I preferred this style but I don't mind a spy parody but I feel like any attempt at this would fail because *Austin Powers* exists. 

I liked that scene actually. I felt it made it funnier. I think it was also foreshadowing the fact that she'd been brainwashed. It was her mind trying to understand what was going on. 

The film starts by explaining that the bad organisation was involved in assassinations, election fraud and other stuff. Yeah, it's pretty vague and a lazy set-up but they were definitely bad guys. 

I don't really know to be honest. Maybe people just like popcorn fare books in that universe. 

It did seem a little forced but I got it myself. The movie kind of presents itself as a novel, right? Every novel needs a romance. 

Same. I definitely think character development was secondary to the action and story. Which is a weakness of Vaughn's entire filmography in my opinion. I liked Sam Rockwell's character though, I thought he portrayed it really well. 

The needle drops were there to remind us of the *Kingsman* films I think. I didn't mind them tbh but they could have been better placed. 

Yeah, that seemed strange to me too tbh. It didn't suit her, a nice red dress would have fitted her style better I think. I think it was just so they could have the "if we can't have reality, let's have fantasy" line. Or maybe the wardrobe budget ran out and they thought; "let's just let-out Dua Lipa's dress and reuse it".
You were using snarky humour and it flopped.
